item.title: Luncheon of the Boating Party
item.lesson: On a restaurant balcony over the Seine at Chatou, just outside Paris, Renoir assembled everything he loved: friends, wine, sun through an awning, and the easy mixing of classes that defined the new leisure of the 1880s. Everyone here is a real person — seamstresses, journalists, painters, a bureaucrat's son in a top hat, the restaurateur's children. The young woman at lower left cooing at her terrier is Aline Charigot, whom Renoir would marry. Around them, one of the great still lifes hides in plain sight: bottles, grapes, and glasses painted with such pleasure you can almost hear the table. Renoir was fighting his private doubts about Impressionism's looseness, and you can see him having it both ways — faces modeled with care, everything else dissolving into light. Duncan Phillips bought it in 1923 for a record price and built America's first museum of modern art around it; it has anchored the collection ever since.
item.lookFor: Trace the gazes around the table: nearly every glance lands on someone who is looking at someone else — a round of unrequited attention that keeps the party circulating forever.
